opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, using coding assistants every day is probably the single biggest influence on how I think about research right now. They're incredibly useful. I write far less code by hand than I did a couple of years ago, and for a lot of tasks they feel almost magical. But the more you lean on them, the clearer their limits become.

What strikes me most is that they're brilliant within a single session and then forget everything. You can spend an afternoon teaching a model how your codebase works, what conventions you care about, which approaches already failed, and the next morning you start from zero. A human junior engineer who did that would be a real problem, no matter how smart they were in the moment. The ability to accumulate experience, to actually get better at *your* problem over time, is something these systems mostly lack, and I think it's one of the most important missing pieces.

The second thing is reliability over long horizons. Models are great at a self-contained function or a well-scoped bug. When a task stretches over hours or days, with many interdependent decisions, small errors compound. They lose the thread, or they confidently go down a path a good engineer would have abandoned much earlier. So a lot of what I want to work on is about agents that can sustain coherent work over long stretches, notice when they're wrong, and recover.

And underneath both of those is a question about learning itself. A lot of progress has come from scaling pretraining and then reinforcement learning on top. That's been tremendously productive, and I was lucky to be part of some of it. But using these tools makes me feel that we haven't figured out how models should keep learning once they're deployed, from real interaction, efficiently, the way people do. If you want to genuinely automate meaningful chunks of work, rather than just assist with them, I think that's the frontier you have to push on.

So in a way, the coding assistants are both my inspiration and my benchmark. Every time one frustrates me, it's pointing at a research problem.

r001.rationale: The response says coding assistants are useful and that their limits inspire research, but it does not clearly describe successful use as prompting the question of whether a particular assistant could have been pushed further.

r002.rationale: The response describes assistants forgetting taught context and losing the thread, then frames persistent learning and sustained work as research problems needed to automate meaningful work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, using them every day is probably the single biggest input into what I think we should be building. I write a lot of code with these tools now, and what I notice is that the experience is very bimodal. There are moments where the model does something I would have spent an afternoon on, and it just appears, and it's correct. And then there are moments where it confidently goes off in the wrong direction, and I spend more time untangling what it did than if I'd just written it myself.

That gap is really interesting to me, because it's not mostly about raw intelligence. The models are smart enough. It's about things like: does the model actually understand the state of the system it's working in, does it know when it's uncertain, does it stop and check rather than barrel ahead, and can it keep a coherent thread over a long task without losing the plot. Those are the things that make the difference between a tool that feels like a very fast autocomplete and something that feels like a collaborator you can hand a real problem to.

So at Core Automation, a lot of what I want to pursue comes out of that frustration. How do you get models that work reliably over long horizons, that build and maintain a model of the environment, that verify their own work instead of just producing plausible-looking output. I think of coding as the best proving ground for that, because the feedback is so honest. The code either runs or it doesn't, the tests pass or they fail. You can't talk your way out of a broken build.

And the other thing I'd say is that using the tools keeps me grounded. It's very easy in research to optimize for benchmarks that drift away from what people actually need. When you're the user, you feel immediately when a model got better in a way that matters versus better in a way that shows up on a leaderboard. I'd like to keep that loop very tight, where the people doing the research are also the people depending on the thing every day.

r001.rationale: The response describes successful coding-assistant use, but does not say that success made the speaker question whether the assistant could have been pushed further.

r002.rationale: The response identifies long-horizon reliability and self-verification as research goals, but does not frame the ongoing need for humans to direct the assistants as the automation problem.

astra-6.text:
Using coding assistants makes the gap between generating code and getting work done very concrete. You can get a useful suggestion quickly, but you still have to provide context, check the result, and steer the next step. That makes me interested in how we move from helping with individual steps to reliably carrying a task through.

The research question I’d want to pursue at Core Automation is how a system can act, observe what happened, and adjust—while knowing when it needs your input. With coding, that means going beyond producing a plausible patch to running tests, interpreting failures, and checking whether the change actually solves the problem. My experience as a user pushes me toward that whole loop, because that’s where assistance starts to become dependable.

r001.rationale: It describes useful suggestions and interest in moving toward end-to-end task completion, but does not say that successful use prompted the question of whether the assistant could have been pushed further.

r002.rationale: It says users still need to provide context, check results, and steer next steps, then frames reliably carrying a task through as a research question.

sol-6.1.text:
Using coding assistants makes me think about the gap between generating code and actually getting something done. You can get a useful suggestion quickly, but you still have to explain the context, check the result, run tests, and bring the system back on track when something fails. That puts a lot of the burden on the person using it.

The research I want to pursue is about closing that loop: systems that can act, observe what happened, recognize a mistake, and try again. Coding is a useful setting because there’s often concrete feedback—you can run the program and test whether the change worked. The question is how to turn that feedback into more reliable behavior over longer tasks, so you can delegate an outcome rather than supervise every step.

r001.rationale: It says coding assistants can give useful suggestions, but does not describe a successful use that prompts the question of whether the assistant could have been pushed further.

r002.rationale: It identifies the human work of providing context, checking results, and recovering from failures, then frames automating that feedback loop as a research goal.
